name: Dana Haddad

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Dana, thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or any party. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Linden Hill, a small mixed farm with 80 dairy goats, a cheese room, an apple orchard and some hay fields. I milk the goats at six and four, make cheese two days a week, and look after the orchard in season. I also run the farm's online shop, which I set up myself with AI tools, product photos, descriptions, the lot. I love the cheese room, it's quiet and precise; I don't love trimming 80 sets of goat hooves.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my partner Rami in a rented cottage on the next farm over. He's a software tester for a company in the city, working from home most days. We paid a deposit on the cottage and he's still paying off his student loan, so we've got maybe three weeks of savings. I use AI every day, for the shop, for planning the cheese batches, even for checking goat symptoms before I call the vet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's useful but overhyped, which is what I'd say anyway. It saves me hours on the shop, it doesn't milk goats. Most people would shrug.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, the farm's margins are tight with or without AI. The Linden family could close the cheese room any year if feed prices jump again. That's my real worry, not robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using AI to grow the online shop, maybe add a cheese subscription. I'd ask the Lindens if I could sell cheese at the Saturday market for a cut. And Rami and I would try to save his monthly bonus.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine, a bit stretched. Normal life, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How tight is the farm, really?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last winter feed went up a third and the Lindens didn't pay themselves for two months. When feed prices jumped last winter, the Linden family stopped paying themselves so they could keep paying me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a cheese subscription look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Monthly box, three cheeses, a jar of apple chutney, delivered. AI can write the emails and handle the orders, I just need to make the cheese. If 100 people signed up, it'd cover my wage twice over.

think: The farm's **margins** are tight regardless of AI.
The Lindens could close the **cheese room** if feed prices jump.

Sell cheese at the **Saturday market** for a cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's good for small farms like ours, because we can do the office work without hiring. But I'd also say it's tough on people like Rami. I'd say both.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My side is fine, goats need hands. But Rami tests software for a living, and that's exactly the checking work AI takes first. If his firm cuts testers, we lose more than half our income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push the cheese subscription hard so the farm earns more and can pay me more. I'd help Rami move toward something less exposed, maybe the farm-tech side, setting up AI shops for other small producers. And we'd keep 50 a week aside from now on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, mostly for Rami. I'm okay, he isn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Rami that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say you've built half my shop, you can build ten more for other farms. My partner Rami tests software for a living, and checking software is exactly the kind of work AI eats first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're okay. How sure are you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty sure for the next few years. The goats don't care about software. But I'd be the one paying the rent, and I earn less than him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say be practical, there's no point shouting at it. Figure out what still needs a human. I'd also say the government needs to help people like Rami, quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rami's job is gone by 2028, probably sooner. My job holds until robots come, maybe 2031, and then a robot milks goats for less than me. In two years we go from two incomes to one, and in five to maybe none.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd make the farm shop fully AI-run, so the Lindens need fewer hours from anyone but me. I'd cut everything, Rami's car, the streaming, the gym. Rami would look for any hands-on job locally, the orchard, the cheese room, even the hay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. It's like a goat kidding wrong, you know you need to act fast but you're not sure what's right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the gap between thinking AI and robots help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It gives us three years where my hands are worth something and his head isn't. For three years my goat-milking hands would be worth more than my partner Rami's university degree.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever consider leaving farming?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the robots came for the goats, yes, but to what? Every job I'd consider gets the same robots. I'd rather own a bit of a farm with robots than work for someone else's.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years, I'd say there's time if you start now. Small farms could actually do well, robots get cheaper. That's what I'd tell the Saturday market lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With five years, Rami could switch before his job goes. And I could try to buy a stake in Linden Hill before robots arrive, while it's cheap. The Lindens are in their sixties and have no children who want it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the Lindens about a partnership, buying in slowly from my wages and the subscription money. Rami would retrain toward farm tech or anything hands-on. We'd save hard, even 100 a month, for the stake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but there's a plan. That makes all the difference.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you afford a stake on three weeks of savings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Slowly, a share of the cheese profits each year instead of a pay rise. The Lindens would rather sell to me than to a developer. The Linden family would rather sell the goat farm to me, a bit at a time, than to a developer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Isn't buying into a farm risky if robots are coming?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Owning the farm is safer than working on it. If the robots come, the owner gets the savings and the worker gets a letter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, I'd say it's actually good news for small farms if they plan. Robots will be cheap enough for a goat farm. I'd say that confidently.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be fine, honestly. I'd have time to buy in, bring in robot milkers, and grow the cheese side. Rami would have time to move into something new.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Start the partnership talk with the Lindens this year. Grow the subscription to 200 boxes. Look at robot milkers once they're proven on other goat farms, and plan for a baby when the income's steadier.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. Hopeful, even.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A baby. Is that tied to all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, completely. We want kids, but not while we're both on thin money. With ten years' warning, Rami (her partner) and I would have a baby once the cheese money is steady, not before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could still go wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The Lindens could change their minds, or feed could spike again. AI doesn't stop a bad winter. But I'd have a plan, and that's most of it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because Rami loses his job first and then I lose mine, with no time to buy into the farm. What would help is cheap loans for workers to buy into the farms they work on, and help for people like Rami to retrain.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about owning things. When the robots come, the people who own the goats will be fine, and the people who milk the goats won't be.

headlineQuote: When the robots come, the people who own the goats will be fine, and the people who milk the goats won't be.
portrait: Dana is 27, milks **80 goats** and makes cheese at Linden Hill, and runs its AI-built **online shop**.
She lives with **Rami, a software tester**, whose job is far more exposed than hers.
She's pragmatic, uses AI **every day**, and sees **ownership** as the way through.
Her mood is driven by **Rami's risk**, peaking as alarmed in AGI by 2028.
With time, she plans to **buy into the farm** and start a family.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, when **Rami's job** goes first and hers follows before she can **buy in**.
whatWouldHelp: **Cheap loans** for workers to buy into farms.
